The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 27, consideration in committee of Bill No. 78, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944-Mr. Abbott-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Limitation of amount of liability to bank.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
On Tuesday, when the house was good enough to give the bill second reading a little ahead of schedule, we had quite a wide discussion on the details of this legislation, but there were one or two questions which I asked to have stand over with the understanding that I would answer them now.
The first point was raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia, the hon. member for The Battlefords, and I believe the hon. member for Prince Albert, on the matter of banks requiring the deposit of title as security against some loans. In the regulations under this act the conditions are defined under which these loans may be made, and it is provided that the banks may, in certain classes of loans, require title, as the hon. members pointed out. In addition, section 6 of the regulations provides that in cases where in the opinion of a responsible officer of the bank further security is required or deemed advisable, the bank may take such further security as a responsible officer of the bank considers appropriate in the circumstances.
I have made inquiry as to how often that provision was taken advantage of, and I find that it is done mainly in the frontier areas; in the Peace river district of British Columbia and Alberta, in northern Saskatchewan, in the interlake area of Manitoba, where the actual loan is generally made either for the clearing of the land or for the building of small barns. In those cases there is little chattel security to be obtained. In such circumstances the banks have asked in some cases for deposit of title. In the case of the hon. member for Assinaboia, most of the loans in his riding, according to my records, seem to be for implements, and it is not a common practice there. In the case 
6 the bank may ask for deposit of such title. The bank is not compelled to make the loan; the farmer is not compelled to accept the loan.
The next question was by the hon. member for Prince Albert and the hon. member for Greenwood, followed up by the hon. members for Melfort and Souris, suggesting that, while the act has worked very well up to now, perhaps the top limit on loans of $3,000 for ten years could be raised. At the time I pointed out that my figures did not seem to indicate very much pressure on that ceiling, because the average amount of the 170,000 loans made is $980. But I was asked whether I could obtain a table showing the number of $3,000 loans, and the hon. member for Prince Albert also asked whether I could have a sample prepared for one district. That was a little more difficult, but since he asked it I had the sample prepared for the area around Prince Albert. Once again, I do not know whether there is much interest in the details of the table; it is not very long. In our office the loans are classified by provinces, by banks and then in the five classifications for which loans can be made. These $3,000 loans are listed in that way, by banks, by provinces, and by class. Since the inception of the act in 1945 the number of loans of $3,000 total 2,214, or roughly 1 [DOT] 3 per cent of all the loans made. That would not indicate very much pressure on the present ceiling.
It is a little difficult because of the way in which the records are kept, to ascertain what is the medial loan, though the average is around $980; but examination of the amounts for one province by one bank shows that the great bulk of the loans range between $300 and $1,500. Of the loans, eighty-five per cent are for the purchase of agricultural implements; most of the small loans seem to be for the purchase of low-priced items such as binders.
So far as this table is concerned, if there is interest in it I can ask to have it appear in Hansard. If there is not that interest, hon. members who are concerned may see it for themselves.

speechtext: I was not here the other evening and I should like to ask a couple of questions. Last week in reply to a question I placed on the order paper, I was informed that no branch under the farm loan board had been set up in Newfoundland, as the number of requests did not warrant it, and that requests from Newfoundland were now being handled by Ottawa direct. Could the parliamentary assistant tell me how many requests have been received, and what are the mechanics by which these requests are handled now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I can answer the hon. member in this way. We are not now discussing the farm loan board act; this is the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It is true that the farm loan board has no facilities in Newfoundland; but the actual handling of transactions under the Farm Improvement Loans Act is done by the branch managers of the chartered banks in Newfoundland. So far there have been only two loans in Newfoundland, but that is a matter for the branch managers. Just as a matter of interest, I can find out what progress has been made so far as the farm loan board is concerned and communicate it to the hon. member.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I would appreciate that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
As I said when the resolution was under discussion I think this act has been of great service to many farmers in this country, but even around my own constituency I occasionally run into farmers who are not aware that they may obtain loans under it.
I would like the parliamentary assistant to explain to the house what the department does to inform farmers of the existence of this legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Greenwood asked a similar question Tuesday evening, and at that time I told him the principal source of information had been the branch managers of banks themselves, when farmers came to inquire as to loans. I suppose it is quite true that many farmers do not go near banks because they do not think they could get loans. I also said that we had put out one or two small pamphlets. Since then I have checked, and find that all told we have put out four small pamphlets in the last six years. In the expenditures for the present year, however, we have an item-and I say 

this with perhaps some reluctance to the hon. member for Greenwood-of $9,000 for publicity for pamphlets setting out very briefly the provisions of this legislation and how farmers may secure help. I think the most striking fact we could quote in that pamphlet would be the astounding increase in service from 4,300 loans in the first year of operation to 59,000 loans last year; but I think this is a field where it would be a real help to the farmer if a little more publicity were given by the board in pamphlet form, rather than through the banks. The farm associations have been most helpful in spreading word to their members, but perhaps in this case even the hon. member for Greenwood may agree that there is justification for a small expenditure for a pamphlet to tell the farmers what they can expect under this act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Is it absolutely a necessity that the applicant have title to his land before he can qualify for a loan under this act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I must apologize to the hon. member. I shall need the aid of my assistant on these detailed questions, and he has not yet appeared. Would the member just hold that question for a moment?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Could the act be
extended a little to service the country north of the Peace river? This loan board does good work in the more settled areas, but in new areas where the buildings and fences are not up to the same standards as they are in Ontario, for instance, and the farms are removed from large centres of population, the inspectors take a very stern view of the situation and often refuse loans. I know of one case where a loan was refused to a man who had cleared five hundred acres of land and who needed a loan in order to purchase seed and tools. He had exhausted his cash in clearing this large area. The farm loan board could not see its way clear to lending him any money. The excuse given was that the man was a bachelor, and he was over sixty years of age. We might provide him with a wife and set him up in a good home, then probably he would qualify for the loan. The fact was that the man had a good reputation for paying his debts; he was a practical farmer and therefore a good risk.
I believe the act should be extended, so that these new areas could be given just as careful attention as the more settled areas.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
In reply to the member for Cariboo, I should like to point out that we are not considering the Canadian Farm Loan Act but the Canadian farm improvement act. Actually, the record of this act in outlying areas is even better than it is in the established areas, as is shown by the table I filed last Tuesday night. It is in the Peace river

district, northern Alberta and Saskatchewan, that the loans for the clearing of land and improvement of buildings have been most successful.
As I pointed out to the member for Assiniboia, in those areas they often ask for security by way of the deposit of title. The Farm Improvement Loans Act has no connection with the Canadian farm loan board, which is an organized body lending funds on land. The Farm Improvement Loans Act is simply a means by which the Canadian government guarantees the credit extended by the banks for farm improvements, and the bank managers are the ones who pass on the farm loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I am not one to
advocate advertising the lending of money to farmers. I think that the farm loan board does good work, and so does this farm improvement act. I still believe, however, that even the trust companies refuse to lend money on lands on the north side of the Peace river in British Columbia that are profitably cultivated. These properties are regarded as poor risks simply because they are fifty miles away from a railway. Farms can be operated successfully in spite of the fact they are some distance away from large centres of population. I believe that both the banks and trust companies could extend their lending operations in this part of the country, in which there are worthy people who are good risks and who should be given a little financial assistance.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I wish to thank the parliamentary assistant for the answer he gave to my question. I do not object to the practice of the banks in frontier areas asking for the deposit of titles for a loan for the improvement of land or buildings, because there is not much else in the way of security that could be given to the banks. I do say, however, that I believe the practice, which is quite prevalent in my locality, of asking for the deposit of title on a farm implement loan, should be frowned upon. The banks have adequate security. Up to about ten per cent of the aggregate loans are guaranteed by parliament. To show that that guarantee is worth a good deal, one needs only to mention that out of $170 million of loans, claims have been made by the banks for only $19,000.
In addition to the ten per cent guarantee on farm implement loans the bank takes a lien on the farm implement. In my opinion that should be adequate security. I believe one of the reasons why the banks in certain areas are asking for a deposit of title is the fact that they are faced with competition from credit unions. The bankers take the attitude that if they can get the farmer to
Farm Improvement Loans deposit his title he will not be eligible for a loan from the credit union. I wonder if the parliamentary assistant would explore the possibility of having credit unions brought under this act, so that they would be eligible for the same ten per cent guarantee. If that were done, then I imagine that the practice of the banks in certain areas of requesting a deposit of title on farm implement loans would be discontinued.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: My question was, is it necessary for the applicant to have a clear title to his property before he can qualify under this act?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I believe that the farmers all
across Canada are grateful for the passage of this legislation, and will appreciate having it extended for a further term. I am supporting it, but I -want to go a little further. The latest figures we have from the dominion bureau of statistics show that approximately twenty-five per cent of the people of Canada are living on the land. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Will the
parliamentary assistant say whether there is a quota for each province?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
There is no quota for each
province, nor is there a quota for any one of the banks. It is just a matter of the business risks available in the various provinces for loans by the various banking institutions.
So far as the point raised by the member for Assiniboia is concerned, I rather think he defeated his own purpose when he mentioned the strong competition between the credit unions and the banks for this type of business. If there is any competition, the banks would not put any block in the way of getting the business. His second point was whether or not credit unions could be included in this act. This problem we discussed three years ago when the act was first reviewed. Two points were raised immediately. First, this is a federal act, and the ten chartered banks of Canada are controlled
790	HOUSE OF
Farm Improvement Loans by federal legislation and inspected by federal inspectors. Credit unions are under provincial authority and control.
A third point, perhaps not so important in these times as at other times, is the matter of solvency. The institution lending the money must be solvent, just as the farmer who is borrowing the money must be solvent. The ten chartered banks of Canada are certainly much more secure than the great variety of credit unions across this country. Some credit unions are in excellent financial shape. Others are in not too strong a position. It is for that reason, for simplicity of operation and the fact that under this federal act we have federal control of the banks, that the guaranteed loans have been restricted to the ten banks chartered under the federal government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

Mr. Wismer, and it is doing excellent work all through the province, particularly in the northern areas.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: In the table submitted by the parliamentary assistant the other day I notice that the loans made to farmers in British Columbia were roughly eight per cent of those made to farmers in Alberta and Saskatchewan. I was wondering what was the reason for that. I believe that the government's intent is sound and that they will bend over backwards to help the farmer, but to what extent are the banks co-operating? The question is this. Has the parliamentary assistant the figures indicating the amount and the number of loans applied for and the number rejected or not granted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
This table I filed on Tuesday evening was one which I ' was quite sure would arouse great interest when it was actually printed, because the three prairie provinces are far ahead of the other provinces, despite the great size of the agricultural industry in Ontario and Quebec. There are reasons for that. In the three prairie provinces the farms are large in size; the farmers use expensive mechanical equipment; and there are also many new farms. The clearing of land, the improvement and the extension of buildings is an important factor with regard to the prairie farms. In Ontario and Quebec, on the other hand, the farms are for the most part much smaller; there is not the same need for the large mechanical equipment, such as the combine that is used in the west. More than that, the farms in the east are much older. They have had fifty years or a hundred years of careful husbandry over the farms, fences, houses and that sort of thing, which undoubtedly is one of the main reasons for the great difference in the number of loans in the prairie provinces as compared with those in the old provinces of Ontario and Quebec. As to British Columbia, the agriculture industry there is fairly well limited to two or three areas; and the area represented by my hon. friend from Yale did not qualify quite as easily as did the prairies until this amendment I mentioned the other night, which included the planting and purchase of fruit trees.
As to the number of applications which have been refused, we have no official record of them. The situation here is the same as that with regard to most business loans made by a bank. The record is of the loans made, not of the loans refused, because of the very nature of the application. The farmer or businessman goes in to see his bank manager

and talks over the problem. From that conversation he can soon see whether it will be possible for him to obtain a loan or not.
However, we have a much better way of estimating the number of rejections, and it is this. Of all people in Canada I believe the farmers are the ones who are the most vocal in complaining when they think they are suffering from an injustice, and the administration would certainly be the first to get letters from farmers complaining about the matter if this act was not working in the way it was intended to work and many applications were refused. Second to the farmers in the matter of complaint would be the businessmen in these communities who have been put on a cash basis, as has been said, by this act. In the third place, and perhaps most important right here, we would certainly have heard from members of parliament. I raised that point with the administration and I found that, for example, in the last year, only three members of parliament had brought cases of refusal of loans to the attention of the administration; the explanation in each of those cases was perfectly satisfactory to the members concerned. So I would think that there is not much in the way of refusal of loans where there is reasonable security, remembering that we have this ten per cent guarantee by the federal government.

In the explanatory notes to clause 2 I find the following:
The period during which guaranteed farm improvement loans may be made expires on February 28,	1951. The proposed amendments
extend this period to February 28, 1954, and also increase the aggregate amount of farm improvement loans that may be guaranteed.
I checked back on the original bill which was passed in 1944. Section 5 of that bill reads as follows:
The minister shall not be liable under this act to make any payment to a bank in respect of loss sustained by it as a result of a farm improvement loan made after the aggregate principal amount of guaranteed farm improvement loans made. by all banks exceeds two hundred and fifty million dollars or made more than three years after the commencement of this act.
Farm Improvement Loans
I beg your pardon; that was the amendment as of 1948. The original act is just the same; it deals with the amount of $250 million. The explanatory note in this bill says the amendment is to increase the aggregate amount. But still this section in the amendment mentions $200 million. The parliamentary assistant to the minister stated the other night that this amount was to be increased. It appears to me as though there has been a decrease. Can the parliamentary assistant explain that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: On the surface, it looks as if there had been a decrease. When the bill was first passed in 1944 the amount mentioned was $250 million. At that time it was not known whether the act would be accepted by the farmers, or whether it would work out well; it was a probationary period. At the end of three years it was found that it did not work too well. I remember that the then member for Wood Mountain, now the hon. member for Assiniboia, said that it did not work well because out of $250 million we had lent only $35 million in those three years. The next act, therefore, did not repeat the $250 million but did say, the balance of the $250 million first voted; in other words, loans made in the next three-year period would be for that balance of $215 million-I think it was $35 million for the first three years, and the loans were limited then for the whole six years to that first $250 million. Now the rate of lending has increased greatly. Last year it was around $63 million. Although there is some $30 million left over of the first $250 million total loans, we made a fresh start and said that for the next three years the total loans on which we would pay a ten per cent guarantee would be $200 million. Although it seems to be a contradiction, the fact is that in the first three years we made $250 million available. Actually, the amount of guaranteed loans for the first three years was $35 million. The amount in the next three years was $135 million; therefore the total of the first six years was $170 million of the $250 million provided. Now we are dropping all mention of the original guarantee; for the next three years we are going to make the $200 million available for loans in this period of three years, of which we guarantee ten per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: What would the indication be if you took the rate of increase of the last few years and projected it three years forward?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

I have the actual table here. That would be the best way of showing it. The last three years was as follows: $30 million, $45 million and $63 million, a total

Farm Improvement Loans of $130 million odd over the last three years. So that it looks at the moment, especially with those minor restrictions on credit which we are now making, as though $200 million will be all right for the next three years. If it is not-

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
You can
always come back and ask for more.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

speechtext:
What happened to the $80
million which was not taken up in the first six years? Was it put back in the treasury?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Has the government taken into consideration at all the increasing of the maximum loan from $3,000 to a greater amount, say $4,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: We had quite a discussion on that on Tuesday night, and at the beginning of this discussion I pointed out that consideration had been given to it. I do not think there is any need at the present time to increase the $3,000 limit. I am thinking mainly of the purposes of the act. In Saskatchewan, and in the prairie provinces, in regard to machinery, the most expensive implement on the farm is a $5,000 combine. I think almost any farmer who contemplates buying a $5,000 combine feels that he must have $2,000 cash before he can buy such an expensive implement. If the prices of machinery keep going up and up and if inflation stays with us, before very long that $3,000 ceiling may be too low. I think the same thing would apply to the $200 million total ceiling on the loans that may be made in the three years. The sum of $200 million is enough for the coming year, and certainly I would think it is enough for the first two years. In the third year, if prices

continue to rise, and there is at the same time a reasonable production of farm implements, lumber and building materials, the $200 million may need to be increased toward the end of the three-year period.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDINC ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: While the fact that the average loan is $1,000 does seem on the face of it a complete answer to the suggestion that you should raise the limit above $3,000, does it go further than that? speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, February 23, consideration in committee of Bill No. 24, to confer certain emergency powers upon the governor in council-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1 Short title.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in keeping with the great importance of the subject matter with which this bill is concerned, the debate which took place on the second reading was of a high order, if I may express that opinion. The only regrettable feature of it was referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that is that we did not have with us to add the important contribution which he always made to discussions of this sort the former member for Kinder-sley, Mr. Jaenicke. I was very saddened one day when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar told me that Mr. Jaenicke was extremely ill. I immediately wrote Mr. Jaenicke a long chatty letter about some of
Emergency Powers Act the legal problems which had arisen here only to find with dismay that about a day after it had been sent his death was announced. I am sure that everyone regrets his passing, because in dealing with matters of constitutional law he made a contribution which was not excelled by that of any hon. member on either side of this house.
The main policy issues of this bill have been pretty well covered. They may be discussed again and if they are I should like to reply to any further criticisms that may be made. It will expedite discussion in committee if I deal at this time with certain specific criticisms which were directed against the bill, largely by the hon. members for Kamloops and Eglinton. Inasmuch as the matters they have raised are related to a greater or lesser degree to one another it might perhaps be expedient for me to deal with them all at the same time.
The first criticism was that this bill might lead to an unwarranted invasion of provincial rights. In that connection I will perhaps be labouring the obvious by pointing out that the bill is manifestly brought forth as a result of the creation of an emergency which threatens the security of the nation. That emergency makes it imperative that measures should be taken in the interests of national defence. The defence which is involved in this bill is not only the defence of the federal government but of all provincial governments and of all citizens of Canada. I do not see how it can be logically argued, as long as the orders in council which are passed under this bill, if it becomes operative, are confined strictly to the powers granted under it, that this will be an invocation of powers by the governor in council which may be regarded as an encroachment upon provincial authority.
If this parliament, which is specifically empowered by section 91 of the British North America Act to deal with matters of defence, cannot in this emergency invest the governor in council with authority to deal with such matters as come under the heading of defence, although they may in another aspect come under provincial jurisdiction under the heading of property and civil rights, then we would have a constitution which would be unworkable indeed. The granting to the federal governor in council of jurisdiction to make defence preparations contemplates the giving to the governor in council of authority to deal with precisely the kind of emergency with which we are now confronted.
The second criticism was that the bill provides for an unwarranted interference with individual rights. This argument was developed by both the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Eglinton. As I
794	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act understood their remarks, they were based upon the omission of the word "arrest" from the specific powers excluded from the act. The War Measures Act provides in effect that the government may by order in council provide for the arrest, detention, exclusion or deportation of any person. This bill omits to include in the powers granted any provision for detention, exclusion or deportation of any person. Indeed it goes on to exclude those powers, but it does not exclude the power of "arrests". Whereupon my friends drew the inference that there is something sinister about the omission of the word "arrest" and that the government instructed the draftsman of the bill to leave out the word "arrest" in order that it might retain the power of arrest by executive fiat and in that way invade the liberty of the subject.
The reason for that omission is neither sinister nor mysterious. It was not an oversight because the matter was considered carefully by the draftsman of the bill. The reason the word "arrest" was omitted from these exclusions, thereby leaving the power of arrest with the governor in council, will be made clear if hon. members will look at the bill itself. They will see that in section three there is a provision for the creation of offences by order in council, the offence of violating the orders which the governor in council may make pursuant to this act. The governor in council has the power to provide that individuals may be fined or imprisoned for not obeying the orders and regulations made pursuant to the powers conveyed by this bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think the minister will agree that it is not confined to that matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I quite agree. This is a customary provision, not only in statutes of this parliament but in provincial statutes. The lieutenant governor in council or the governor in council are empowered to make regulations and provide for their enforcement. Obviously if one is going to create a hew offence it will not be worth while unless some provision is made to enforce it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the minister give us an illustration of the type of provincial statute to which he is referring?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would not like to undertake to quote with accuracy, but my impression is that in most provinces there are regulations made by the lieutenant governor in council dealing for example with the operation of dairies and prescribing certain rules of sanitation. Such regulations would provide that if there is a breach of the regulations certain steps will be taken to enforce them. I am sure my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, from his wide knowledge


of provincial administration, must recollect many examples of regulations of that kind which have been made.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I will not interrupt the minister again on this, but I must confess that I cannot remember any provincial legislation conferring any such powers as those contemplated in this section.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But making regulations-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, but not making regulations of this kind.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: -accompanied by provision for their enforcement. Let me ask my hon. friend a question. Does he not recollect that regulations are made under the Ontario health act-I do not know whether that is the proper title-by the lieutenant governor in council?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There are a number of provisions for regulations relating to administrative responsibilities under acts of a nature which call for adjustment from time to time to, shall we say, the ordinary practices and circumstances that must be met. What I am pointing out is that in this case the rules and regulations are rules and regulations that obviously contemplate the declaration of severe penalties for as yet unstated offences, and the word "arrest" relates to all these. I know of no similar provision in any provincial statute, and I was simply asking the minister if he could illustrate it by reference to some provincial statute he has in mind in that respect.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am sure I could turn up
the exact reference but speaking from memory, and confining it to the province with which I am most familiar, I would say we had in the province of Manitoba-and I am sure my hon. friend can recollect the same thing in the case of the province of Ontario-very elaborate health regulations that took up a good deal of space in pamphlets put out by the government. If my memory serves me rightly there was provision in those regulations for their adequate enforcement. Whether or not those provisions provided for arrest I would not like to say at the moment, but certainly they provided for fines, and if I remember correctly they also provided imprisonment in certain circumstances.
At any rate in this particular case, as the leader of the opposition correctly states, the powers which are being conveyed are of a wider and more important character perhaps than those which are ordinarily exercised by the lieutenant governor in council in a province. When they are being conveyed-and to take a counterpart, under the

War Measures Act they resulted in the wartime prices and trade board-obviously provision must be made tor their enforcement, and it would be rather absurd if in providing for imprisonment no provision was made for the arrest of the offender.
May I point out that where the power of arrest is continued but not any longer in juxtaposition with the power of detention- which is not given by the bill-not any longer as an adjunct to detention, when a man is arrested under the power that is under discussion here he is arrested only for the purpose of being brought to trial in the ordinary way before the ordinary courts with all of his rights of habeas corpus and all of the other safeguards which are thrown around the liberty of the individual.
With deference, I think the confusion has arisen in the minds of the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Eglinton because they have failed to distinguish between arrest as an adjunct to detention and deportation and the law which contemplates the withdrawal-I will confess under conditions of war-of individual liberties by executive fiat; but arrest in its present context is merely a part of the necessary method of enforcement of the order in council that may be passed pursuant to this bill if enacted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If the minister has confidence in that argument why does he need to retain in the governor in council the power to make orders in council with respect to arrest when he is not asking for the power to make orders in council with respect to detention, and when under section 3 of the bill power to prescribe penalties by way of fine and imprisonment is vested in the governor in council?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think I can answer that
question quite definitely. They say we should table everything. I believe there are important reasons why the view they have expressed is quite erroneous. Under the act it is provided in effect that orders-what kind of orders?-of a legislative character shall be tabled in the house. The first steps usually taken under a bill of this sort are orders in council of a legislative nature, because they provide for the set-up under which the regulations that may be passed will operate. Thus an analogue of the wartime prices and trade board, for example, when it gets in operation under these orders which are legislative in character, will make subordinate regulations. One of the emanations of the wartime prices and trade board had to do with rent control, and it made thousands of separate regulations or orders dealing with what was to happen as between John Doe and Richard Roe in reference to what rent is to be paid for a certain house, what extension was to be given and so on. Surely it is fair to the members of this house and to everyone concerned to provide, as this bill does, that the orders in council that are legislative in character shall be tabled, and that on balance it would be unwise to provide, even from the standpoint of parliament, that the legislative orders parliament might wish to check should be cluttered up with a myriad of executive regulations in which this house would not be interested.

Emergency Powers Act
So far as any denial which may result from the invocation of the powers granted under this bill by the governor general in council is concerned, that will be an order in council which is legislative in character and it will be tabled in parliament. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I wish to make some observations under this section, because it is under section 1 that there can be made the general comments which would embrace the various sections of this act. At the time the resolution was before the house, which resolution had the effect of bringing into the house the bill itself, and while the bill was not yet before hon. members, the Prime Minister in his remarks indicated that it was desirable that this bill should place before this house and before parliament their responsibility for legislation and for what would be done. Following his remarks I expressed my own approval of the thought that had been expressed by the Prime Minister, to the effect that parliament was to be called upon to exercise its responsibility, and that parliament was to have the opportunity to deal with whatever measures were -to be taken. I am not attempting to quote the exact words but I think what I said accurately summarizes the effect of the explanation that was given and of my comments at that time.
We now have the bill before us. When the resolution was under consideration the prime Minister made it clear that it was intended to introduce this bill because the government did not desire to invoke the War Measures Act. I followed the Prime Minister and agreed with what he had said about the desirability of seeking to impress, in every way possible, upon the minds of the people of our country the fact that war is not inevitable and that what we are really trying to do at this time is to prepare those measures of defence which may assure peace. To the extent that any action by this government, properly taken, would produce this result,
I believe I indicated my own approval.
We have the bill before us now, and the wording of it. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that there is no reason for this bill to be introduced at all. This is in effect the War Measures Act, subject only to the limitations which are largely illusory, except to the extent that I shall mention, and the provisions under which orders in council might be annulled if the government decided to concur in the views expressed by any hon. members who indicate it should be annulled.
I hope I made it clear before that 1 was not suggesting the War Measures Act should be invoked. I do not think it should be invoked, and I do not think we should be called upon now to pass a bill in this form. As far as the question of granting emergency powers is concerned, I think there is general agreement that, under proper definition and


proper limitation, certain emergency powers undoubtedly will be necessary. For that reason the principle as to whether emergency powers shall be introduced is not the point in issue so much as the details within this bill, and the wide open powers that are conferred, so similar to the War Measures Act.
Let us see exactly what this bill does. Let us see to what extent it in any way limits the authority of the government to a greater extent than would the War Measures Act itself. Section 2 provides that:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, as he may by reason of the existing international emergency deem necessary or advisable for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
Except for the restrictions contained in subsection 2, and the provision in subsection 4, which makes it possible to take certain proceedings in this house and in this parliament for annulment, that is simply a wide open declaration, similar to the declaration contained in the War Measures Act. Nothing has yet been said either by the Prime Minister or by the Minister of Justice which gives the slightest indication to hon. members as to what parliament is being asked to do, other than simply to say that except for these very limited restrictions the government can do anything that it deems necessary at any time to meet whatever circumstances arise out of this emergency. That after all is precisely what the War Measures Act permits, and therefore the only thing that is before us, other than the wide open powers of the War Measures Act, is the effect of the limitation and the practical possibility of annulment referred to in subsection 4 of section 2. Subsection 2 (a) provides that the powers conferred on the governor in council shall not include the power to make orders or regulations in relation to detention, exclusion or deportation of any person. The word "arrest'' contained in the corresponding provision of the War Measures Act is not excluded, as has already been explained by the Minister of Justice.
As the Minister of Justice has pointed out, the word "arrest" then relates to the power of the governor in council to prescribe penalties by way of fine, by way of imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or by way of both the fine and such imprisonment. That after all brings together the word "arrest" and the provisions in subsection 3 for penalties that might be created.
The Minister of Justice says than anyone arrested, after having been charged with an offence created by an order in council under section 3 of the bill now before us. would

have available the habeas corpus procedure, or any similar protection of the individual. I cannot see how it is possible for the Minister of Justice to argue, in view of what has already been done on other occasions, that the governor in council under this bill, if it becomes law, would not be in a position to declare that habeas corpus shall not apply to any proceedings taken under section 3.
The Minister of Justice smiles. The Minister of Justice, however, is well aware that under the same general powers of the War Measures Act, habeas corpus proceedings were suspended by order in council. There is nothing in this bill to suggest that the government would not have similar power in relation to any proceedings under the section set up.

speechtext:
Would my hon. friend permit me to make a correction? I am sure that he does not mean to indicate what is not the fact. If he will look at section 2 of the bill he will see that it reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything contained therein, the powers conferred on the governor in council by subsection one do not include power to make orders or regulations in relation to (a) detention, exclusion or deportation of any person. . .
That is expressly excluded from this bill, and it was expressly included in the War Measures Act. That is the difference.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That has no relationship whatever to the proposition I am now putting forward. What that provided for in the War Measures Act was that an order could be made detaining individuals, as was done in a number of cases, and excluding or deporting persons where that was deemed advisable. But in this particular case, if the detention is detention upon the basis of a charge under the ordinary proceedings, then I submit there is nothing in this bill that would prevent an order in council being made which would declare that in the case of detention under any order in council passed as a result of subsection 3 habeas corpus proceedings would not be available to those detained under orders made within that section. That is what I am submitting. It certainly does prevent the sending of people into concentration camps as was done by this government without trial in many cases under the War Measures Act. But I submit that it does not prevent orders which would deny certain protection, once the steps have been taken to lay a charge in accordance with whatever penalties might be imposed under section 3 of this bill if it becomes law. Such orders would lay down the procedure or rather would deny the effect of some other act.
The Minister of Justice will recall that many orders were passed under the War Measures Act which contained the phrase,
Emergency Powers Act "notwithstanding the provisions of such and such an act", not habeas corpus alone but other individual safeguards. It was quite a customary procedure under acts very similar to this for the government to pass orders in council which stated clearly that notwithstanding the provisions of any other act certain things could be done.
I agree that under this legislation a charge must be laid, that the charge would be laid under whatever order was passed under section 3. If bail were permitted1 a man might be free to leave just as he would in an ordinary case. The question of habeas corpus would not apply. But for the sake of argument let us assume that the court regarded a case as being a serious one and imposed bail that practically meant it was impossible for it to be provided. That has been done at times with the knowledge that that will be the effect. I submit that there is nothing here to prevent the passage of an order in council which would provide that some other act of this parliament shall not apply in such proceedings. I am not going to go further than to put that proposition forward in the conviction that that is so and that there is no restriction which would prevent that being done.
We come now to the next exception in section 2, subsection 2(b), which provides that there shall not be power to pass orders or regulations in relation to censorship or the control and suppression of publications and writings. Undoubtedly that provision is desirable, but I would point out that it would be very easy to introduce a bill giving such protection without passing a bill of this kind simply for that purpose. I would think that such a provision is a highly desirable one.
On the other hand, I would point out that if the government is not going to deal with things of that kind there is all the more reason why the government should bring down very soon in this session, because of the emergency which the Minister of Justice has described as grave, some legislation which will make it possible for the government to deal with those subversive communist publications which are seeking to undermine the thoughts of newcomers to this country in languages that they can understand better than the two recognized languages of this country.
The very fact that the government, properly, is limiting its power in regard to censorship and the control and suppression of publications and writings, and by that very fact in this emergency would deny itself the opportunity to deal with these subversive

Emergency Powers Act publications put out in languages which perhaps can be understood only by many people who have just come to this country and who desire to become Canadian citizens, does indicate the need for immediate action along that line. I leave that thought with the minister.
I would point out once again that simply to provide such protection as this for the press and for individuals in this country did not require an only slightly modified form of the War Measures Act which is now before us.
The third limitation is contained in section 2, subsection 2(c), which provides that the government may not make orders in council or regulations in relation to expenditures of money other than in accordance with an appropriation by parliament except expenditure of moneys from any fund or account established by order or regulation in connection with a scheme of control for the purposes of that scheme of control.
If the Minister of Justice can explain that section in more understandable words I feel sure the members of this house would like to know what is intended to be done under this section, no matter how little they may know about what the government intends to do otherwise. In so far as I am able to read this mumbo-jumbo, it simply means that the government is free to set up any fund of any size for any purpose it declares, and then having set up such fund or funds the government shall not be free to spend other moneys apart from those funds which are not provided for by an appropriation of parliament.
Unless there is some limitation which I am unable to read into that rather involved wording, it simply means that at any time the government wishes to have funds available apart from those provided by appropriations in parliament they can create a fund so large and under such terms that they could carry on anything they wished to carry on without this limitation really having any practical effect. If that contention is true it seems to me that the exceptions are very important. Certainly the real exceptions that are made could have been introduced in some declaratory bill and could have established the rights of citizens in that respect.
The other point is the question of annulment. This is an illusory protection. After forty days, no matter how important the order may be, proceedings may be taken, if parliament is in session, by way of resolution to seek the annulment of a particular order. What happens during the extended periods when parliament is not in session? Orders having profound effect upon the freedom of the individual and the whole economy of

this country could stand unchallenged and there would be no procedure of which I am aware by which the members of this parliament would have any opportunity to exercise any measure of authority over what had been done. I submit that if, as the Prime Minister said, we wish to deal with legislation in this house with the thought that this emergency is one which may extend for a considerable period we should retain the parliamentary procedure of our democracy as much as possible.
Then I suggest that this War Measures Act only slightly restricted is not the bill to bring before the house but rather that we should have a bill telling us exactly what the government intends to do. After all, one of the most important issues in this struggle- and it has been said by those with knowledge and authority that the struggle may last for ten, twenty, twenty-five or even fifty years- is whether we are going to retain the processes of democracy in reality, whether we are going to carry forward the business of the country by the rule of law, or whether because of the emergency we are going to abandon these practices and for long years place in the hands of the government undefined powers which have not in any way been stated or worded by the members of parliament.
I repeat that, subject to these minor limitations and the illusory protection afforded by section 2, subsection 4, the bill simply says in effect that because of the emergency the government can do anything that it thinks should be done. I cannot see where that is an overstatement. I do not know where there is any restriction on the generality of that statement in this measure. Certainly the extent to which orders under the War Measures Act, so similar to this-in fact with exactly similar wording-were upheld, indicates how wide the powers are.
What is the government asking parliament to pass? It was indicated that if the government decided to adopt any measures of control it would be under this legislation that they would bring them into being. The government has indicated that if a national registration of manpower is undertaken by it it will be under this act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It could be under this act. I was asked if the act would be sufficient in terms to allow it to be done. There was no statement that it would be done under the act. I was replying to a question whether the terms of the act would be broad enough to cover that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The answer of the Prime Minister, as he now says, was that it could be done. I must confess that the interpretation

I placed upon that was what I have now said, that if it were to be done this would be the act because I was not' aware that the government had indicated that it contemplated any other legislation. I recall the very clear, and I thought very understandable, statement of the Prime Minister that events might bring about the exercise of any of these powers under this act, and I do not know of any other act under which it could be done.
I wish to leave no interpretation on the Prime Minister's words beyond what he himself has placed upon them, but it seemed to me that was the reasonable interpretation in view of the absence of any other legislation under which it could be done. We now have something new in our minds. The Minister of Justice has referred today to a board. What board? We do not know. The act does not say. There is no statement as to what board he has in mind. Therefore any remarks that he has made about what the board would do, or the kind of regulations that would be brought before the house, involve undefined orders relating to an undefined board which would be called upon to deal with an undefined subject, and that is supposed to be responsible government at a time when the responsibility of government to parliament is in fact the essence of the very struggle in which we are engaged today.
In dealing with the points that had been raised, the Minister of Justice spoke of what had been said about the extent to which the bill would make it possible for the government, by order in council, to disregard any of the ordinary constitutional limitations upon its authority over those things specifically placed under the authority of the provincial governments by the British North America Act. As I recall his words, he sought to emphasize that in a grave emergency of this kind it was not just defence of this house or defence of this government that was involved but defence of the provinces and of the people of Canada.
Again, if this emergency in fact is an emergency that may continue for years to come, then what happens to this constitution that was going to be rewritten? Are we to have no real constitution for possibly fifty years except the discretion of the government from day to day? That would be the result. What is the effect on the discussions that have already taken place? I submit that the provincial governments, which now have under consideration certain financial proposals as an alternative for the taxing powers conferred upon them at confederation, simply could not know whether the amount proposed would be adequate or 80709-511
Emergency Powers Act inadequate because under this act the dominion government could at any time pass an order that would have a profound effect upon the revenues of the provinces. Therefore the fixed amount which they would receive would not tell them whether or not they were going to have enough to carry on their business if they did not know what was going to be available to them from the remaining fields of taxation.
Let me give a clear illustration. For the sake of argument let us suppose that the government under this act, as it could, passed regulations with respect to the amount of gasoline that would be available for motorists, or passed regulations as to the use of automobiles. Immediately that would have a direct impact upon revenues available from that particular source, and the remaining taxes available to the provinces, in addition to the amounts now under consideration, might change greatly as a result of the passage of some order of which they would be wholly unaware until the federal government had already made its decision.
Again, let us assume that the government decided to exercise its emergency powers with respect to the amount of alcoholic beverages that could be produced or sold, not an impossible consideration. If they did that it would have a very considerable effect upon the revenues of all provinces. The minister may say that no such thing would be contemplated, but I would be interested in what the province of Newfoundland, so recently joined with the rest of us in one nation, would think of the possible effect of an act of this kind upon the agreement which defined their rights and made certain pro; visions which could be made relatively ineffective as a result of other things done under this legislation.
I suggest that if we are going to show our people that we can carry forward democracy in the face of this threat, the first place to make democracy operative is right here in this house. The first step we should take in tackling that first line of defence of our democracy is to make sure that the members of this house, who represent the people of Canada, do in fact have the opportunity to exercise their judgment and discretion as the representatives of the people as to what laws shall govern this country. I think it is for the members of this house to know, with a measure of clarity we do not now have, exactly what powers the government is really asking and what they have in mind. If they have in mind the wide powers of the War Measures Act, why bring in that act with only a couple of hairs cut off the tail?

Emergency Powers Act It is the same animal with just a slight clipping, which has not greatly changed its appearance or anything about it.
This is not just something for us to pass over lightly. This is not just something put forward by the opposition because, as the Minister of Justice indicated, they sometimes feel it their duty to raise objections. I am putting this forward with the utmost earnestness in the belief that perhaps the first duty of the members of this parliament, next to the assurance of forces in being to meet such obligations as this country has assumed or will assume under its collective responsibilities, is to make sure that government by the people is a reality. Government of the people by the people is a reality only when the representatives of the people decide on the laws that are going to affect the lives of those who sent the members here. I would point out that when our neighbouring democracy-which it is perfectly true has a system very different from ours but which nevertheless is founded upon the basic principles of democracy which came from Magna Carta-introduced	emergency legislation,
they said what boards they were setting up. Congress was asked to decide whether certain bodies would be created for the purpose of dealing with the affairs of the people represented by the members of congress. The bill in the United States, which would deal with some of the powers that have been suggested as possible powers to be exercised under this act if it becomes law, consists of more than 900 sections. I am not mentioning that fact to suggest that the length of the document necessarily indicates how good it is. I do point out, however, that when the members of congress, representing people who live lives so similar to ours in an economy very much more like ours in many ways than that of any other country in the world, considered that legislation, they knew what they were doing. The members of congress knew what powers they were conferring upon the government. What remained to ibe decided was the administrative authority of those bodies that were to be set up.
Here we are simply left in the position that we cannot even guess what the government has in mind). Some people, perhaps wrongly, interpreted the remarks of the Prime Minister in an earlier debate as indicating that the government was considering the possibility of price and other controls; and as I understand it this was the legislation under which those controls would be brought into effect if that should be done. Since that time, however, through a speech by the Prime Minister at the Chateau Laurier and) a speech by the Minister of Trade and'

Commerce at the Royal York hotel in Toronto, hon. members have learned1 that there are very definite limitations as to the intentions of the government in this respect. The press has been very helpful to us in that regard. We now know, if it has been reported correctly, that it is not the intention of the government to introduce controls of that kind unless we face something in the nature of general war.
If that is so, it would: seem that we do not need; such wide open powers as these. If the government has something else in mind, we should be informed. And if the government has something else in mind, why does not the Minister of Justice instruct his draftsmen to put into understandable sections exactly what it has in mind^ and then let the members of this house exercise the judgment they are supposed to exercise as to whether this government shall have this power? I conceive that to be the basic principle of democracy that we are trying to preserve. After all, whether or not we are inclined to realize it day by day, this is the place in all Canada where the kind of democracy we have in this country is to be determined.
Right now we have before us a bill that suspends our constitution at the whim of the government and leaves the members of this house with no measure of authority over the laws that are to affect the lives of our people in very important ways. That is so with this exception, that if the house is sitting, and only if it is sitting, after forty days we may have the privilege of introducing a resolution which would annul any step which might have have been taken. I hope I may not be criticized as cynical if I suggest that the Minister of Justice has given a fair indication of just how much we might hope to accomplish with a resolution of that kind. The Minister of Justice does not take kindly to even courts disagreeing with his legal opinions. When he is so unwilling to accept the decision of the court which has been enlarged by this government to become the court of final resort to which the people of Canada may appeal and seeks stiff to go to the privy council, which he regarded as an emblem of colonialism only a short time ago, can we expect that he will be greatly inclined to listen to arguments which might be put forward here by any hon. members who may disagree with the opinions that he has expressed?
I was interested in the statement he made today that, while perhaps it was not his role to give legal opinions, nevertheless he was going to do so. I suggest it is his role. I suggest that, as Minister of Justice and *attorney general, it is his duty. I also suggest

it is equally his duty to be prepared to listen to other arguments, and to be willing to place before his legal draftsmen the suggestions that may be made, and not to indicate to the house, as he has this afternoon, that with the wise judgment of this government it is most unlikely there would be any different result if a resolution came forward. I would say, in view of the statement he has made, we could pretty well wipe out any thought that section 2, subsection 4, is intended to have any real effect. In any event, it would not have any effect during a considerable part of the year when orders of immense importance might be made while the house was not in session.
The Minister of Justice is also anxious to create the impression that the government has not any thought of going so far as it could go under the War Measures Act. If that is so, then I suggest that much more extensive limitations be included than those now put forward. I repeat my contention that if this house is to be an instrument of democracy, which is government by the people through the thought, judgment and expressed opinion of the representatives of the people, then this act should go back, and it should go back on the decision of the Minister of Justice himself. We should have brought before us an act which really tells what the government has in mind, what powers it is really conferring, and what the government will do. It is not only that we should want to know what the government will not do, but many of the members of this house want to know what the government is going to do about a number of things of immense importance. Unless there is a change in the attitude of the government we are simply going to be told that is not for us. This all-wise government is going to decide.
The furthest the curtain has been pulled aside from the secrecy of that exalted body, the government of Canada, is that the minister has referred to an undefined board dealing with the affairs of this country under undefined powers and exercising those powers for an undefined period and to an undefined extent. Now, Mr. Chairman, if that is democracy, then it is time the textbooks on democracy were rewritten. I suggest in real earnestness to the Minister of Justice that there is no urgency in regard to the exact date on which this bill passes. Unless the government is prepared to say there is something being held up, and tell us what it is, then he should advise his draftsmen to present a truly democratic bill to this house
Emergency Powers Act so the members will know what the government is going to do, and what powers we are asked to confer upon the government.

speechtext: I do not want to make a speech about this, but there are certain points which evidently the leader of the opposition has overlooked. He held up to us the terrible prospect that this world may be facing a long period during which this emergency condition may persist, and that by this bill, for the whole of that period, parliament was going to suspend the Canadian constitution. If the hon. member had read the fourth section of the bill, which has to do with its duration, he would have found that the act will expire on May 31, 1952.

speechtext: I will give no such undertaking; but I will give the undertaking that if it is done parliament will have to do it. It will not be done by the government.
