speechtext: Will the Prime Minister tell us that parliament will know any more then than it does now concerning the powers the government will exercise under the bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would hope that parliament and its members would know as much as the government knows about the future of this world. It is one of great uncertainty, and one in which it would be, I believe, presumptuous for anyone to say, what is going to be his course for the next year or any indicated period of time. This government has not that presumption.
The hon. member says the exclusion of the right to deal with detention would not exclude the possibility of taking away by order in council the right of habeas corpus. If the hon. member will just reflect upon what habeas corpus is, he will see that it is a high court judge saying: have the body of so and so whom you are detaining brought before me so that I can look into the causes of his detention and decide whether or not that detention is legal. Then, if the hon. member will read the bill, he will see that no regulation whatever can be made in relation to detention. I believe it is quite evident that any regulation that may be made affecting the right of habeas corpus would be a regulation concerning detention. Habeas corpus is essentially something in relation to detention, and is nothing else.
806	HOUSE OF
Emergency Powers Act
The hon. member says that after forty days there can be a resolution of annulment. I believe that was probably a lapsus linguae. It is within forty days of the tabling of the order in the house that the resolution can be made. If hon. members feel that period is too short and it should be extended beyond forty days, we will have no objection to that.
With respect to the other matter that was raised, I believe by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, he will recall that last year we passed the Regulations Act. In that act it was provided that every regulation-making authority shall, within seven days after it makes a regulation, transmit copies of the regulation ini English and in French to the clerk of the privy council. Thereafter it is the duty of the clerk to publish those regulations in the Canada Gazette, and it is the duty of the government to table them here within fifteen days of their publication in the Canada Gazette. According to the act "regulation" means:
. . . a rule, order, regulation, by-law or proclamation (i) made, in the exercise of a legislative power conferred by or under an act of parliament, by the governor in council . . .
It was provided then, and explained, that we were trying to use the broadest possible language so that it would be only those things about which an order of exemption was passed that would not have to come under the terms of this statute, and any order passed exempting a regulation or an order in council from the terms of this act has to be tabled. We had a serious discussion over that, as to whether it was proper that we should require the government to tell parliament that there was something that was not being tabled, and as to whether security might be endangered in that way; and we came to the conclusion that, at the present time, we would take the risk; and that if there was anything that we thought should not be brought to the attention of parliament, we would have to pass an order and bring that exempting order to the attention of parliament. We would try to draw that order in the form that would do the least harm to security. If there were questions about it, we would try to explain to those who were asking the questions, if we felt that we could not give the explanation openly, what it was all about and why we were not being more specific. For my part I felt hon. members would show understanding if we had to withhold something, referred to it in rather vague terms and explained to hon. members who raised any question about it why we were not going to be more explicit. If they did not show such understanding, any who did not would take the responsibility. I did not think there was


any member of parliament who was going to be anxious to take the responsibility of doing anything that might in any way be harmful to our national security.
Although the bill is drawn to apply only to orders in council-the requirement to table applies to everything-we might all feel happier if the provision for the annulling resolution could extend not merely to orders in council, but to all that comes within the term "regulations" under the Regulations Act. I do not think the government would have any objection to that. We want to bring these things to parliament and, of course, we will be doing only the kind of things that we believe parliament is not apt to repeal. We may make mistakes. We would not be human if we were not susceptible of making mistakes. We must table all these regulations and I do not know but that we might be disposed to accept an amendment, that the right to move a resolution to repeal would apply to any regulation even if not made by an order in council. In the last war regulations were made which were quite as important as anything we did by orders in council. Otherwise I think we would want to do everything by order in council.
At this time we cannot say to what extent these powers are going to have to be exercised. Th leader of the opposition says that there might be orders in council when parliament is not in session. It may be that there will be things which should be done when parliament happens not to be in session. Otherwise we would have to keep parliament in session all the time. World conditions are susceptible of rapid changes. I do not think a government would be acting properly towards parliament if it made any major decisions when parliament was not in session and did not quickly call parliament together.
I think that the power to act should be there. I hope it will not have to be exercised, but I think that the power should be there so that it could be exercised. Whenever it is exercised, whether it be in the form of an order in council or in the form of a regula-tion^ my personal opinion is that it should be subject to this proviso: if parliament frowns upon it, parliament should annul it. I think perhaps it will be possible, when we reach this section, to have it modified in such a way that the power to annul would apply to anything that comes within the definition of a regulation of a legislative character contained in the Regulations Act passed in the regular session of 1950. We attempted to make the definition allinclusive, so that everything would be brought to the attention of parliament. We took the security risk of leaving that to

apply to everything that might be done under this bill if it becomes law, in spite of the fact that there might be some things that, for security reasons, we would not want to publish broadcast. But we would have to exempt them, and we would have to bring the exempting order here. Once again, I express the hope that, when we bring an exempting order here, an hon. member would seek to get information privately with respect to any exempting order, before raising the question publicly in the house. By following that procedure I am sure we will not have any trouble about security. I am sure that no hon. member who obtained information privately would want to make it public unless he felt it was ridiculous to withhold the information on security grounds.
With respect to the extent of the powers, it would be a much easier thing to do if we could come here and say: This is what is going to have to be done and nothing more is required. That would be a much more satisfactory situation, and I would have been much happier last night if, in another capacity, I had been able to give that kind of information to an audience I was speaking to. They would also have been much happier. But that is not the kind of world we are living in. If parliament thinks that we can be trusted under these restrictions-and the restrictions provide that we shall not go beyond what is required in the circumstances -then parliament will give us those powers. But with the possibility of various things that we just cannot determine at this time having to be done, in order to meet the changing conditions, I suggest that the powers have to be drawn in fairly broad terms. We did not want them any broader than the Department of Justice told us was enough. But what they say is this: These things mean restrictions on some individuals and they are subject to contestation before the courts. It is therefore important to have the language so broad that the courts will not say: "You have gone beyond what parliament authorized you to do." I am sure there is contained here a good deal that goes far beyond what will be done by order in council or by regulation. But the Department of Justice feared-at least, that was the advice we obtained from the permanent officials-that if it was not drawn in the broad language that already had had the scrutiny of the courts and had been upheld by the courts, they would not guarantee that it would stand contestation. We were convinced that we should stay on the safe side and be able to support the legislation.
The hon. member referred to the restriction with respect to the expenditure of money in a special fund. Any special fund would
Emergency Powers Act have to be created by parliament, or it could be the kind of fund that arises out of an equalization scheme. In the case of controls and the establishment of quotas, that sort of thing existed during the last war. There were equalization funds that had to be apportioned to the producers of certain commodities in respect of the prices higher than our ceilings that they obtained on the quotas they were allowed to export. The exception in the restriction provided in the bill has to do with things of that kind. We were told that was the way to express it. It is not very elegant language, but that is the way we were told to express it if we wanted the Department of Justice to say that it would be successfully supported against any contestation.
The hon. member referred to an unidentified board. There is no board that could be identified at this time, and there will not be any board until there is something for the board to deal with. There are certain controllers who have been selected under the act which was passed at the special session, and who will probably be invited to continue as such under the Defence Production Act when it has been passed. If and when we do have to set up controls there certainly will have to be administrative machinery; but so far there is nothing in the mind of the government that could be disclosed to the committee as something that was going to be done.

speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question with relation to the remarks he has just made? I think the Prime Minister will agree that the right of habeas corpus to the average individual is illusory unless he can be visited by counsel who will know the facts and draw the writ for him. Does the Prime Minister say that the inclusion of the word "arrest" and giving to the governor in council power to make orders and regulations with respect to arrest do not allow them to make orders and regulations with respect to restricting the right of counsel while under arrest?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would say, and I think my hon. friend would agree with me, that any interference whatsoever with the rights secured by the old habeas corpus statute would be invalid under a restriction which prevents an order in relation to detention. Any interference whatsoever with the procedure relating to detention would be illegal under this section.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

May I ask the Prime Minister a question? In case any drafting is being done during the dinner adjournment to embody the kind of amendment the Prime Minister suggested might be introduced in section 2, subsection 4, to include regulations

Emergency Powers Act as well as orders in council in the annulment provision, I would point out that the Prime Minister, as well as the Minister of Justice, used the expression, "regulations having legislative effect, or of the nature of legislation." May I say that the Regulations Act does not use any such expression. What it speaks of in the interpretation section, 2 (a), is this:
"regulation" means a rule, order, regulation, bylaw or proclamation
(i) made, in the exercise of a legislative power conferred by or under an act of parliament.
It seems to me it would be a mistake to qualify the word "regulation" if it were introduced into section 2, subsection 4, by any such expression as the one mentioned, namely, regulation "of a legislative nature" or "legislative character." That is not the language of the Regulations Act. It says:
Regulation . . . made, in the exercise of a legislative power conferred by or under an act of parliament.

Emergency Powers Act at this moment I am not so much concerned, speaking practically, with annulling orders as I am to get the government to pass some of these orders. However, the plain fact of the matter is that if we are going to perform our function as a parliament, particularly as opposition members of parliament, we have to retain the parliamentary way of doing things just as much as we possibly can, but if by passing this bill, which I want passed, we are going to give the government the power to pass orders of a far-reaching character I think we have got to retain in the hands of parliament as much power as is needed to annul these orders if parliament should wish to do so.
This afternoon the Minister of Justice in commenting on this matter said two things that were of interest to me. On the one hand he gave us the Prime Minister's assurance that, if a motion should be introduced seeking to annul a government order, the government wouldi see to it that consideration of such a motion would be facilitated. I think the words were to that effect; at least it was in that spirit. The other comment made by the Minister of Justice was that we in the opposition should not think that just because we were opposing something that made it wrong. He said that the majority has rights in this parliament too, and it is so obvious one cannot but agree with him.
But I ask the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister to notice this difference with respect to the annulling of orders compared with the ordinary measures that go through parliament. Usually a bill or resolution or motion is introduced or initiated here in the house, and its passage is decided on the floor of parliament. In that circumstance we on the opposition side may differ with it but if the majority votes for it it becomes law. That is the rule of democracy. But in the case of these orders, although they may be passed by a government, a cabinet, that ostensibly has the confidence of the majority, there has not been a positive vote for them by the majority of the house. This is a case where the process is in reverse. The law is passed first by order in council and it becomes law. It is in effect. That having been done without a vote having been taken on the floor of parliament, it seems to me that special efforts should be made to make sure that if there is any substantial body of objection to it, full opportunity is provided for that objection to be expressed and for votes of the House of Commons and the other place to be taken.
I am not casting any doubts at all upon the assurance given this afternoon by the Prime Minister through the Minister of Justice. I am not suggesting it is going to happen but

prime ministers do change once in a while in the life of this country. People do come and go, and it is also the case that what really counts when we are dealing with laws, parliamentary and governmental matters, is the written word. I should like to see the Minister of Justice go back to the law officers of the crown and see if there is not some way in which subsection 4 of section 2 can be reworded so that it will contain right in its text provision as to how that annulment can be proceeded with on the floor of parliament.

I think we have to give the government powers, and I want the government to use those powers to deal with the present critical situation. At the same time, however, we are a parliamentary democracy, and I want this parliament to retain as much control as possible over the government in the exercise of those powers.

I am quite certain I speak
for all members on this side when I say we were impressed with the fact that in what he had to say this afternoon' the Minister of Justice obviously had given a good deal of careful consideration to the points raised in the debate on second reading. The fact that he should have considered them, and that in certain respects he and the Prime Minister should have made concessions or, to put it perhaps more mildly, indicated that they were prepared to share at least to some extent the views put forward by members on this side, encourages us to think that by making reasonable suggestions we can work out a bill which will be a great deal better than we consider this bill to be, at least in its present form.
For that reason, on the first clause I should like to deal with this bill in general for a few minutes, and particularly with some of the further points where we think there is room for accommodation, room for our views to be given effect ini order perhaps to have amendments made which will further improve the bill. Perhaps I should indicate the approach we take to this matter so the minister will understand the basis for the request we make for a further limitation in the statute on the extent to which these powers may be exercised. It seemed to me that in what he had to say this afternoon the Prime Minister based his case, in asking for our consent to the granting of powers which he admitted were .wider than at the moment they could say would have to be used, upon the principle that in a time like this parliament should say to the government, "Very well. We will surrender to you all the powers you ask in spite of the fact that at the moment those powers may be wider than you can justify."

Emergency Powers Act
I take a rather different approach to that question. We are agreed that the times are extremely serious and urgent, and that there is an emergency. This emergency has not yet been narrowly defined. It is an emergency, however, which calls upon us to grant emergency powers, and that is a departure from the normal. The normal procedure is that laws interfering with the liberty of the subject, laws taking away from the individual rights we have won over the centuries, can be passed only by the representatives of the people, that is by the parliament of Canada. That is where the residue of power lies as between the cabinet and parliament; and I do not believe we should be asked to surrender powers beyond the actual requirements of the moment. When a case is made out I believe we should surrender now those powers required; we should agree with the government that they must take those powers, and we should place no obstacles in the way. But I do view with grave misgivings any assertion of a principle which seems to me, at any rate, to imply that the government is entitled by the mere fact that there is an emergency to ask for and receive powers which the government itself admits go beyond what can be justified at the moment.
I trust the minister will appreciate that we hold this view in all sincerity; and I think he will understand why we say, no specific case having been made out to show to what extent these powers are required or are going to be used, we believe we should seek to limit this bill, to limit those discretionary powers which normally belong to parliament, to the extent to which you and we can agree it is absolutely necessary to grant them now. Having been successful in writing in those limitations, if the government then should meet a situation in which they need more powers, I am convinced that they have only to make out that case and the necessary further powers will be willingly granted.
The first and most important limitation that occurs to me as being necessary in this bill is a limitation protecting the traditional right of the individual to have recourse to the courts. We can find instances where, though the intention to interfere with the liberty of the individual in that respect is not written into the statute, nevertheless that power has been given in words very, similar to those which have been used to effectively deny the right of action on the part of an ordinary man or woman in Canada who is aggrieved by the act of some controller in the exercise of these powers. I do not mean just put out, or to suffer some imaginary loss, but someone who is actually injured by an excess of authority on the part of a controller appointed under

a regulation or order in council passed pursuant to emergency legislation. There was a clause in the order in council setting up the wartime prices and trade board, and this was a type of order which was repeated a number of times throughout the years, providing that no member of the board and no administrator acting on behalf or under authority of the board shall be or become liable to any person in respect of any act or omission of himself or any other person in the exercise or purported exercise of any power, discretion, or authority, or in the performance or purported performance of any duty conferred or imposed under these regulations or under regulations for which these regulations are substituted, or otherwise conferred or imposed by order in council. A provision of that sort, Mr. Chairman, effectively denies the right of an individual to have recourse to the courts.
I am not talking here about powers that may be taken to control industry, to limit profits or anything of that sort that affects big industry. I am talking about the ordinary man and woman, because if these powers are exercised to the full extent the regulations made do not just affect the big fellow, they affect the ordinary man and woman of Canada, who is perhaps more vitally concerned than anyone else in the preservation of the right to have recourse to the courts. If the right to question in the courts any action or omission on the part of a controller is lost, then one of the fundamental freedoms enjoyed in this country has been lost. We are now being asked to surrender into the hands of the government very sweeping powers. There are only limited opportunities for parliament to question the exercise of those powers by the government. There is one institution open to the ordinary man and woman, an institution which is normally, along with parliament, the custodian of the liberty of the individual; one institution which has traditionally enjoyed independence, and to which the ordinary man and woman has always been free to go in order to assert and protect his or her rights, and that is to the courts.
What we are doing here, if we give powers to make such regulations as the one I have just read, is to remove that other safeguard on the freedoms and rights of the people, a traditional safeguard under our system, by refusing to allow an individual to appeal to that institution. I certainly feel that before this bill passes there should be written into it, not any provision which will prevent the government from taking such action as it needs to control whatever it needs to control, but a provision which will prevent it

from passing such orders in council or regulations as will needlessly and dangerously interfere with the liberty of the individual by taking away his ordinary right of recourse to the courts.
Then I feel there should also be a provision in this act which would restrict the right of the government to pass an order in council denying the right of any individual to be represented by counsel when he is accused of some offence against an order or regulation. The reason I say that, Mr. Chairman, and I ask you to bear with me for just a moment, is not that I am anxious to protect the rights of lawyers. In this country we have seen cases of this in connection with the right of habeas corpus, that right which affords an individual an opportunity to protest against unjust and unlawful arrest or detention. We have seen instances in which, without actually indicating or providing in express words that the right of habeas corpus was no longer to be exercised, it has been effectually removed by the simple provision that the person arrested shall not have the right to be represented by counsel. It is not of much use to the ordinary man, who may find himself innocently or unsuspectingly up against some provision of these regulations which he did not know about, to say to him that the right of habeas corpus has not been suspended. As the Prime Minister has admitted, even the government can make mistakes. If the government can make mistakes, then certainly the controllers appointed by the government can make mistakes. It is quite possible that some innocent man or woman may find themselves under arrest as a result of an action or omission mistakenly taken by one of the controllers.
Under those circumstances that man or woman would be most anxious to exercise the right of habeas corpus. The Prime Minister has said that under this measure the right of habeas corpus cannot be taken away. Mr. Chairman, I have seen examples of the right of habeas corpus being taken away by the simple expedient of denying the individual the right to be represented by counsel. It is not very much help to an individual to be told, "Oh, no, you have not lost your right to habeas corpus," when that person has no idea how to exercise the right and the one person who can tell him how to exercise it and take steps to exercise it is not allowed to interview him. It does not prevent the government from exercising the controls it needs to exercise, but I feel it is absolutely essential that we should protect the right of the individual from wrongful acts or omissions, and the consequences of those wrongful acts or omissions, by ensuring to him that the agency through which he exercises that right, the
Emergency Powers Act counsel of his choice, may not be denied to him. That principle can be written into this bill without derogating from any of the powers which the government wishes to take.
I believe that at this point I can call to my support an address given in this city on Tuesday by a person who, I presume, has the admiration and respect, if not the confidence because he is not in a government position, of the members on the government side of this house. Certainly, he was asked by that party to address them at their annual meeting just concluded. Professor Corry delivered an address in which he asserted the principles which support the stand I am taking. I shall read from pages 12 and 13 of the official text of his address, where he said:
Second, when the government regulates the varied activities of millions of people in detail, it is not humanly possible for a few cabinet ministers and members of parliament unaided to prevent the oppressive operation of rules and regulations. Third, the wider the powers of government are over a long period, the more government attracts men who like to exercise that range of power.
I do not know who was in the audience, or upon whom he had his eye at that time. I simply remind you that he was addressing an audience of Liberals in this city, an audience whose members constitute the government. He went on to say:
While we may feel quite secure in the hands of our rulers today, we can have no such assurance for the future. So it is vitally important to look to the safeguards of individual freedom.
This parliament has long been the prime safeguard of individual freedom and it will continue to be as long as it can insist, as it has in the past, on maintaining its right to pass laws having an effect on individual freedom. But there is that other body which has been the safeguard of freedom, namely the courts. I most earnestly urge that now, at a time when this parliament is being invited to surrender-and to a large extent at any rate is prepared to do so-its powers, carrying with it a surrender of its function of being the protector of the individual, we should look to it that we leave in existence the right of the individual to have recourse to that other protector of his freedom, namely, the courts.
That can be done quite easily by a simple amendment to section 2 which I think should be moved, and which we propose to move if it should be found that the minister does not feel, and does not indicate at this time that he feels, that some such safeguards as those that I have referred to can be written into this legislation. I have discussed this matter under clause 1 because, in the same spirit which the minister showed this afternoon, I want to lay the suggestions before him and obtain his view as to whether it is possible

Emergency Powers Act to incorporate them into the provision of the statute rather than to move out of hand an amendment-and after all, we are limited; we have not the expert draftsmen the minister has in the department-which in some particular may have some flaw and which, as a result, may not be found to be acceptable. It would be preferable if the minister and the government would indicate that they are prepared1, if they are, to incorporate some such amendment in order to save us reaching an impasse over an amendment which we might move. I think it is also proper to say that we regard this principle as of such importance that we are prepared to move an amendment unless the government can accommodate us in that respect.

Mr. Chairman, I intend
neither to repeat the remarks I made on second reading of this bill on February 23, nor to anticipate some remarks I may have occasion to make during the detailed consideration of some of the clauses of the bill at a later stage. I should like, however, to take advantage of what may be the final opportunity to say in general terms that 1 for one deplore this type of legislation. Before we leave this bill I hope the House of Commons will have realized just how far it is going in committing to the hands of the cabinet virtually all the sovereign legislative powers possessed by this parliament. The exceptions to or limitations on that gift of absolute sovereign power are extremely narrow indeed. They are confined to the provisions-and quite limited ones-of one subsection of the bill.
For my part, I cannot justify the transfer to the governor in council of virtually absolute powers by parliament. We were prepared, as I think were all members in the house, to recognize that the existence of a national emergency calls for the giving to the government of certain extraordinary powers that may be required to meet situations that may confront us suddenly, before parliament may have time to act, or that may arise at a time when parliament may not be in session. But that is an altogether different matter from accepting from the government an invitation to place in its hands virtually all the sovereign powers possessed by parliament.
I have been free to approach this subject with what seems to me due regard for the duty and responsibility of this parliament, namely, to make certain that we do not barter away these fundamental, constitutional safeguards of which parliament has traditionally been the champion. I hold firmly to


the view that when parliament makes transfers of vast areas of its powers to the government, it is in effect placing in jeopardy not only the continuation of our freedom but indeed the whole future of our parliamentary institutions. That is why I for one make no apology whatever for having laid so much stress during this debate on the maintenance of as many safeguards as parliament can write into this bill.
I may say here that I received with no little gratification the expressions that came from the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister this afternoon of their willingness to consider some of the concrete suggestions that were made by my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops, and myself last Friday evening in connection with specific defects in the bill. One is glad to see, on the part of the ministers to whom I have referred, an indication of some willingness to give serious consideration to proposals that are seriously put forward, based upon an earnest attempt to study the bill and to appreciate its significance.
The ministers in question have also indicated their willingness to make, certain changes in the bill, and we shall look forward at a later stage to seeing those changes made as well as others too, I hope; because there are many safeguards that need to be written into this bill, apart from the several as to which the Prime Minister indicated this afternoon that he was prepared to entertain amendments to the bill. But even with all those safeguards and many more, parliament is faced with what should be, to the majority in this chamber as well as to the minority sitting in the opposition, a most distasteful invitation to transfer to the governor in council, with few exceptions, the sovereign powers of parliament. I do not believe that that is the kind of method that will commend itself to others who are watching what is happening in democratic assemblies today as proof that democratic methods are equal to national emergencies and to the stress of grave international situations. The fact that parliament is in session makes it all the more unnecessary, it seems to me, that powers so sweeping should be taken from parliament by the government.
The hon. member for Kamloops quoted an extract from the quite notable speech made in this city two days ago by Professor Corry, the head of the department of political science.at Queen's university, when addressing the Liberal convention in this city. To the extract read by my hon. friend may I add the following passage which, it seems to me, contains words of sound and timely

warning to those to whom the professor particularly directed his remarks, namely the representatives of the Liberal party gathered in assembly. He went on to say:
Since we cannot at present see any prospect of decreasing the powers of government, our most hopeful course is to look for more effective methods of control. As we put large funds and much ingenuity into enabling the government to control us more effectively, we should put some thought and expenditure into new and better ways of ensuring the responsibility of government to parliament and the people. If, as seems likely, we are to have a considerable measure of order-in-council government again, we should also be considering seriously the establishment of one or more committees of parliament to examine, not the substance and policy of orders in council but the effect that the powers and procedures contained in them will have on individual rights and freedoms.
May I interject there, sir, that there are two factors, each of them of ithe most vital importance to everyone who enjoys the benefit of the traditions and the institutions that we possess, two things that go hand in hand, that have historically gone hand in hand, the one the handmaid of the other. The first is the supremacy of parliament; the second, the freedom of the individual under the rule of law. It seems to me that in vesting in the governor in council powers so drastic as are contained in this bill we are placing both of those fundamentals to our freedom in j eopardy.
Professor Corry continued:
We should also be studying how to maintain the influence of parliament over policy and administration. As things now stand, the government is always adopting some new measures of great complexity and administering many old measures of great complexity. For explaining to parliament the success of the old measures and the reasons for the new ones, the government has the assistance of a numerous, able and expert civil service. The opposition is expected to criticize policy and administration effectively without any comparable expert assistance. Members of the majority party in the house are not supposed to oppose the government but they are entitled to influence both policy and administration, and they are expected to explain the government's policy to the country at large. More than ever in the future, the government will need to explain its complex policies to the electorate if it is to get the necessary co-operation. The members of the majority party also need expert assistance which they cannot get from the civil service if they are to exercise their legitimate influence on the government and put the government's case effectively before the country.
We should be considering whether the position and prestige of parliament can be maintained unless each political party is equipped with a secretariat which can then give its party an independent and informed view of government policy and administration. It is difficult to see any other way of restoring the balance that used to exist between government and parliament when governmental policies were few and simple and easily understood by the private member. The biggest objection I see to the proposal is that it increases the number of experts
Emergency Powers Act who find employment, but that is inevitable anyway, and they had better be employed by the responsible political parties than by someone else.
Finally, whatever we might find it expedient to do about these suggested devices, we must be vigilant to protect the right of protest and of individual criticism.
Now, sir, I do not need to go over ground with which those of us who sat in the last parliament are very familiar. Order in council government has been criticized on almost every point. It has been criticized for its secrecy and for the fact that there is no opportunity such as is ensured in the operation of parliament, sitting in public, to bring to bear the full weight of public opinion on questions which are awaiting decision by the legislating body.
We have seen examples of great injustice done during these recent years. We have seen occasions where the power and supremacy of parliament were set at nought. We have seen occasions where the responsibility which the cabinet owes to parliament was set at nought simply because the government possessed, under what was virtually an abdication of parliament in its favour, vast powers.
We cannot, without placing in jeopardy our freedoms and these institutions that we, as members of parliament, are sworn to uphold and maintain, risk the kind of action that may well be taken under a bill of this kind, if powers so vast as these are committed to the keeping of a score of men. Notwithstanding whatever members of parliament may say by way of expression of confidence or lack of confidence in that score of men who hold the seats on the treasury benches, the fact remains that there is something so utterly repugnant to the spirit of parliamentary institutions in literally transferring virtually all of parliament's absolute and sovereign powers to a small group of men that I say, Mr. Speaker, faced with anything short of immediate and compelling necessity, there can be no justification for the vesting of powers as absolute as these in the government; above all, at a time when parliament is in session, and is certain to be in session for some months to come.
What I have said, sir, about the need of adding enough safeguards will be developed, I hope, as we come to the detailed provisions of the bill, but with all the attempts that we may make here, whether successful or unsuccessful, to attach additional safeguards to the control parliament may seek to lay down in this measure, the fact remains, and is inescapable, that parliament ought not to be vesting powers as sweeping as these in the government.

I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton:
That clause 2 (a) of section 2 of bill 24 be amended by inserting the word "arrest" immediately before the word "detention."
The reason for this amendment is that, notwithstanding what was said this afternoon by the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister, with respect, if I may say so, we were not by any means convinced by their argument. If I recall rightly the Minister of Justice said that this power on the part of the governor in council to make orders and regulations regarding arrest would in effect give them no more than what was frequently done under provincial legislation where power is given to the administrative authorities to make orders and regulations which the minister stated carried with them power to make orders regarding arrest.
The minister said then he was quite certain many provincial statutes incorporated such provisions. I do not know whether during the dinner recess he has been able to get an example of what he had in mind but I have not been able to think of any such example in provincial legislation. I think particularly of the type of legislation where regulations are made, the provincial liquor acts, where power is given to make regulations regarding the administration of the act. Certainly so far as I know it is not the case that power is given to prescribe offences or to prescribe the method under which punishment will be meted out. There are administrative regulations as to the enforcement of the act, yes, but not regulations prescribing offences, penalties and the enforcement of penalties. Certainly an order in council prescribing arrest would, it seems to me, be an order in council 
or regulation enacting what could properly be enacted only by legislation, and that is punishment or a step invoking punishment which follows from a breach of the order or regulation.
I am not aware of any case where under any statute, under any ordinary legislative process, power is reserved to executive officials either to prescribe penalties or to prescribe the method by which those penalties shall be enforced. As a rule that is part of the legislation itself. If the government wishes to write into the bill before the house the power .of arrest, if they think that is the answer, that would be one thing, and perhaps a case could be made out for putting it in at this time. But I do not think they should ask us to write into the legislation a power which will enable the government by order in council to provide under what circumstances and how a person shall be arrested. There is the Criminal Code for punishing people who are guilty of crimes or guilty of breaches of statutes. To my mind at any rate, nothing that has been said so far justifies asking at this, time for power to make orders in council providing for the arrest of somebody who may be guilty of a breach of an order or regulation subsequently made under the provisions of this' bill. In keeping with what was said earlier as to the necessity of safeguarding the rights of the individual, so that it can. be done, as it can, without interfering in substance with the powers which the government is asking, I submit this amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this
matter was touched on in debate this afternoon it proceeded almost entirely on the basis of its being a question whether or not habeas corpus was at stake. I do not put my argument with respect to the amendment on that basis at all. Looking at the provisions of the section, it is quite apparent that the government, having deliberately omitted the

word "arrest" from the language of subsection 2 (a) of section 2 of the bill, proposes to take the power to make orders and regulations in relation to arrest. The government is prepared to forgo any request for power to make orders and regulations in relation to detention, exclusion or deportation of any person, but not in relation to arrest.
Under this bill the government does not need the power to make orders and regulations in relation to arrest in order to possess ample power to seek the imposition of penalties prescribed by the act on those who offend the terms of such orders and regulations. There is all the power under section 3, subsection 1, of the bill that is required for the prescription of penalties by way of fine or imprisonment, and for the enforcement of those penalties in any proceedings that may be taken arising out of a breach of any order or regulation passed under the authority of this act. So it is abundantly clear that the government does not require power to make orders and regulations in relation to arrest in order to carry out the enforcement of any order or regulation passed under the act, or to seek by due process of law the punishment of any individual, whether by fine or imprisonment as may be prescribed, who is convicted of any breach of any order or regulation. Therefore it seems to me that the expressed desire of the governor in council to retain power to make orders and regulations in relation to arrest is proved to be utterly unnecessary.
It is father strange that the government seeks this power to make orders or regulations in relation to arrest, but stops short of seeking such power in relation to detention. The argument does not hold water for one minute that the government requires the power to make orders and regulations in relation to arrest in order that arrest may be carried out in cases where it is required in the enforcement of orders and regulations issued under the act. There is the Criminal Code to deal with all cases in which arrest is required. Nothing here takes anything away from the effect of the code or any other statute of this parliament. Therefore, sir, no power to make orders and regulations in relation to arrest being necessary for the enforcement of any order or regulation under .this act, and since the power to make orders and regulations in relation to arrest is capable of abuse-though I am not suggesting the government intends to abuse it but am merely pointing out that power so sweeping and so vital in relation to the freedom enjoyed by every individual in this country is capable of abuse-it seems to me that parliament has no right whatever under present conditions
Emergency Powers Act to vest in the governor in council a power which is at the same time both dangerous and unnecessary.

speechtext: There is no desire whatever to have any arrest other than the arrest that would be incidental to proceedings under section 3. If there is the broad statement that there cannot be anything with relation to arrest resulting from orders under this statute there could be a serious doubt as to whether the initial proceeding by way of arrest could be instituted. The Minister of Justice suggests that instead of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Kamloops there might be added at the end the words, "detention, exclusion or deportation of any person or arrest for any such purpose". That would not be objectionable. But if the word "arrest" is inserted as suggested in the amendment then there would have to be some qualification providing that it does not exclude the initiation of proceedings instituted by arrest under section 3.

Then I see that I have no alternative, Mr. Chairman, but to move that amendment. If I may I should like to speak briefly in support of the various clauses of that amendment.
What we are attempting to do is to have incorporated into the bill a provision which, in the first place, would make it impossible to make orders or regulations restricting the right of appeal or the right of recourse to the courts. I have referred already to the provisions which, in previous orders in council, have been passed under similar legislation,

and which have exactly that effect. An example would be clause 15 of the order in council establishing the wartime prices and trade board regulations, P.C. 8528, as amended by subsequent orders in council, which clearly provided that not only shall a member of the board who acts in excess of his authority not be responsible in the courts for any act or omission, but that no individual shall be able to start an action in the courts by way of any injunction or prerogative writ, to assert his rights or to protect his rights or to seek redress from such injuries. Up to the moment the minister has not dealt with the point which I have raised, and I do not think the Prime Minister has either. The point is that this protection of the rights of the individual would in no way prevent the government from exercising the power which it seeks under this bill, under extremely broad terms, to control our economy. Surely it is not necessary, in order to effectively control the economy of the country, to go so far sis to say that a controller who acts in excess of his authority, or commits some wrong by omitting to do something which he should have done, shall be immune from any action in the courts by the person aggrieved. That is all the first clause of this amendment seeks to do. What it seeks to do is to prevent the governor in council at any time in the future enacting a regulation which would take away from a person aggrieved by a wrongful act of some official appointed under such regulation his right of appeal to the courts.
The second clause is directed to the same object. Clause (b) reads that the governor in council shall not have the power:
To make orders or regulations providing that an official acting in excess of his authority under any order or regulation made hereunder shall be immune from action in the courts by an individual thereby injured.
Clause (c) covers the restriction on the right to make orders or regulations setting aside the judgment of any court. What I am seeking to preserve here, Mr. Chairman, is the rule of law. It is an established principle of the rule that individuals who have rights under present legislation in the present circumstances, and who seek to assert or preserve those rights and succeed before the courts which, along with parliament, are charged with the preservation of our rights, shall not have that right removed ex post facto by legislation which would seek to set aside a decision of the court. We have a pretty fair indication of the extent to which the government is prepared to go in the announcement made recently by the Minister of Justice, as a matter of fact, on February 16, in this house, namely, that if they lost the appeal which the government proposed to take to

At the moment they will have to introduce legislation to accomplish the results the Minister of Justice has in mind. The assertion which was made by the Minister of Justice here, that if they lose the Hallet case under the present law, they are going to introduce legislation to change the law with respect to rights established under that law, is a very dangerous principle to establish. It is because of the danger of the principle, which is so easy to extend and to abuse by order in council, that I have included in here subparagraph (c) which would simply provide that the governor in council shall not in the future be able to make orders or regulations setting aside the judgment of any court.

As to the other matter of whether there should be a reservation of right to sue after the fact if an official does something beyond his authority whereby someone is injured, that may be a proper thing to be tried by the courts. If it were established that he

Now if controls do not require to be administered expeditiously, then they are not required at all. If they are required and if they are the kind of measures that the government can bring to this house in the confident expectation that the house will approve them, then they are measures which will have to be administered expeditiously.
There is nothing in the act itself which would exclude these prerogative writs. With respect to something that the government felt should not be interfered with by prerogative writs, that would have to be expressed in the order that was brought to the house and the house could deal with it as it saw fit. The desire there seems

We think it was the intention of parliament that there should be none of these fortuitous profits allowed in the process of decontrol, and that was done in practically all cases of decontrol. We thought that the way to carry out the intention of parliament when there was a change made in the ceiling price of coarse grains was to vest the coarse grains in the government at the ceiling price that existed, and provide that the former owners might take them back at the new price when it was established.
We thought that was authorized, and we have the support of the law officers of the crown to that effect. The courts decided that, although the general language used in the extension acts was sufficient to include that power, because there had been in the original act an illustration given that was not repeated in the subsequent acts it should be assumed the intention of parliament was to exclude that power. They may be right but if they are right the government made a mistake in the method adopted to carry out the intention of parliament. It did not make any mistake as to what was the intention of parliament. It made a mistake, if that is correct, as to the method it adopted to carry out the intention of parliament. All that was said in the statement made by the Minister of Justice on behalf of the government was that if the courts finally held that the course adopted by the government to carry out the intention of parliament had been a mistaken course we would come to parliament and say, "The courts have said we made a mistake as to the procedure adopted. Emergency Powers Act If that is destroying the rule of law, parliament will not pass the legislation. I am sure we all appreciate the statement the Prime Minister has just made. May I turn now to two other matters in connection with subsection 4. The first has to do with the length of time which may elapse before one of these orders or regulations comes to the notice of parliament. The forty-day period referred to in the subsection has to do with the period within which, if there were an order or regulation tabled in the house, a member may seek by way of notice of motion to annul it. But what about the period of time which may elapse before the regulation or order in council is tabled in the house or comes to the notice of the house?
All this subsection contemplates is that the procedure provided for by the Regulations Act should be followed in every case. The procedure under that act, which was adopted last year and which is chapter 50 of the statutes of 1950, is that within thirty days after an order in council or regulation is passed it must be gazetted in the Canada Gazette. Then, within another fifteen days after being there gazetted, it must be tabled in the house by the government. If the full time provided
Emergency Powers Act for is used, forty-five days may elapse after the order in council is passed before it is tabled in the house. It is only when it is tabled in the house that the annulment proceedings contemplated by subsection 4 can be instituted.
I appreciate that it may not always be possible to table orders in council the day they are made. I do not wish to be unreasonable about this, but I do think that a period of forty-five days being allowed to elapse is grossly excessive when one considers the extraordinary nature of the legislation, and the importance and far-reaching effect of many of the orders in council and regulations that may be adopted under the terms of such legislation. It seems to me that with respect to extraordinary measures of this kind, there is no occasion for passing through the stow and cumbersome proceedings contemplated by the Regulations Act with respect to regulations in ordinary cases. That procedure may be satisfactory with respect to measures that are not passed under extraordinary powers such as are proposed to be conferred by this bill on the governor in council. I believe we must have some procedure that will enable parliament to have immediate or nearly immediate knowledge of the contents of such orders in council and, if not satisfied with them, to be able to institute annulment proceedings as contemplated in this subsection.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the member for Kamloops:

And that section 2 be further amended by inserting between clauses 3 and 5 the following clause:
"(4) Every order in council made under or pursuant to authority conferred under this act shall be laid before parliament within five days after it is made or, if parliament is not then in session, within five days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof."
May I just add this further explanation, Mr. Chairman. If these extraordinary orders in council and regulations are tabled in the house, it is not necessary that they should first be required to appear in the Canada Gazette. That can be done in due course later on, in accordance with the provisions of the Regulations Act. But for extraordinary measures of this kind there should be provision for almost immediate tabling in the house, so that parliament will promptly have knowledge of their contents.

Yes. You will notice that in the concluding lines of subsection 4, where annulment is brought about by resolution of the two houses of parliament, it is provided
that the order in council or regulation__
-shall cease to have effect, but without prejudice to its previous operations or anything duly done or suffered thereunder or any offence committed or any penalty or forfeiture or punishment incurred.
It seems to me that these concluding provisions are extremely drastic. Let us assume that an order in council has been passed which has had the effect of laying down law in that form and attaching penalties by way of imprisonment and fine for a breach. Then let us assume that some individual has committed a breach, has been prosecuted, fined and imprisoned. Then suppose that parliament, on receiving notice-and this no doubt would all be in a short space of time-of the order in council when tabled in the house, takes the annulment procedure contemplated by subsection 4 and decides that it cannot approve the order in council in that form, annuls it, and expresses, let us say, strong disapproval of it. Under this provision, the unfortunate transgressor who has committed a breach of the order in council which has since been annulled is still bound by the sentence imposed upon him. That sentence stands; the imprisonment continues; the fine is imposed; notwithstanding that parliament has in the meantime annulled the order in council.

It seems to me that that is an indefensible situation. I can see that, in certain situations, in order to give sufficient protection to those who are charged with the enforcement of an order in council which is law under this section until it is annulled, there is required some provision that will give clear legal effect to what they have done, in good faith, while the order in council was in effect. But that is no warrant whatever or justification for going on to provide that the annulment shall be without prejudice to the offence, the penalty, the forfeiture or the punishment incurred. It seems to me that if parliament, acting in the exercise of its sovereign rights, decides that it will annul the order in council, then whatever has been done by way of the imposition of penalty, fine or imprisonment should end with the annulment of the main provisions of the order in council. Therefore I should like to move, seconded by my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops:
That clause 4 of section 2 of Bill No. 24 be amended by striking out the words "or any offence committed or any penalty or forfeiture or punishment incurred" in lines 45, 46 and 47.

There is one matter in regard to section 3 that I should like to raise. Section 3 is unlike the provision of section 4 of the War Measures Act in this respect, that while it maintains the same ceiling on the period of imprisonment that may be imposed, namely, five years, it does not put any ceiling whatever on the fine which may be imposed. Section 4 of the War Measures Act, while in similar terms, does place a ceiling on the fine which may be imposed, namely, $5,000. As I indicated to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice in conversation at the dinner adjournment, it seems to me that $5,000 ceiling on the fine in the War Measures Act should be revised upwards. It does not meet the needs of the situation today. Although in the case of a drastic offence the penalty that should be imposed should be imprisonment, not simply a fine, there is the problem of corporations, which may be offenders, for whose offence imprisonment is not a suitable penalty; and in the case of a drastic offence a fine of $5,000 might be quite inadequate. However, while I appreciate the point the Prime Minister made on that occasion, that the order in council or regulation passed under the authority of section 3 of this bill would require to stipulate the maximum penalty that may be imposed, maximum
Emergency Powers Act both as to fine and as to imprisonment, nevertheless it seems to me that in this foundation provision, namely, section 3, subsection 1, from which authority will be derived to write such provisions into orders in council and regulations passed under the authority of this legislation, there should likewise be some clear definition of the ceiling on the amount of fine that may be imposed.
There is a ceiling here on the term of imprisonment. That is a proper limitation. It seems to me there should also be some ceiling in the case of the fine, so that we might carry out our function of seeing that proper limitations are written into extraordinary legislation of this kind.

The difficulty here is that
quite wide powers are being taken by the governor in council to deal with situations that we may not possibly be able to foresee at this time in all their outlines to create controls and in connection with them to create offences. The commission of some of such offences may have serious consequences for the nation, and it would seem that it would be wiser for us at the present time to leave discretion to the governor in council as to what the limitation should be on the matter of a fine, especially having regard to the fact that quite extensive provisions have been made for review of these orders in council by parliament, and most of the suggestions of my hon. friends to facilitate that review have also been adopted.
These orders in council will come here with whatever penalties they do provide, and then we can judge whether the penalties are fair in relation to the offences to which they apply.

I do not want to interrupt the minister, but he has misapprehended what I was referring to. I referred to subsection 2 of section 3 which starts with the words:
Any goods, wares or merchandise dealt with contrary to any order or regulation made under this act . . .
I was pointing out that this is really a rewriting of section 8 of the War Measures Act, but that a portion at the beginning of that section had been omitted. That portion referred to any ship or vessel used or moved. There must be some reason why section 8 of the War Measures Act has been carried in as section 3, subsection 2, but with these deletions.
